solved_1: One down! On the very first move, White already has 20 choices: 16 pawn moves and 4 knight moves.
solved_10: Ten puzzles. After just one move by each side, there are already 400 different positions.
solved_25: Zugzwang, a German word: having to move when you would rather pass. You, on the other hand, keep going happily.
solved_50: With no capture and no pawn move for 50 moves, a game can be declared a draw. In 50 puzzles, you let nothing slip.
solved_64: One square per puzzle! Legend says the inventor of chess asked for one grain of wheat on the first square, two on the second, and so on, doubling each time: it would have taken more than 18 billion billion grains.
solved_100: A hundred! The word chess comes from the Persian shah, the king: playing chess means playing at king.
solved_250: The Lewis chessmen, carved in the 12th century from walrus ivory, were found in 1831 on a Scottish island. Some of the rooks are biting their shields.
solved_500: Gambit comes from the Italian gambetto, a trip of the foot: you give a pawn to make your opponent stumble. Ruy López already wrote about it in his 1561 book.
solved_1000: In 1759, the mathematician Euler studied the knight's tour: visiting each of the 64 squares exactly once. You have done a thousand rounds.
solved_2000: In London in 1851, Anderssen sacrificed both rooks, a bishop and his queen to deliver mate: the game became known as the Immortal Game.
solved_3000: Alan Turing wrote a chess program before any computer could run it. He played it by hand, doing the calculations himself.
solved_5000: At the end of the 15th century, the queen, which used to move just one square diagonally, suddenly became the strongest piece. The new game was nicknamed mad queen chess.
solved_10000: Ten to the hundred and twentieth
In 1950, Claude Shannon estimated the number of possible chess games at about 10 to the power of 120, far more than the atoms in the observable universe. A few are still left for you.
days_1: The start of a great story. Chess is about 1,500 years old: you are right on time.
days_3: Three days in a row! The two-faced chess clock became standard in tournaments at the end of the 19th century; your regularity is already setting the standard.
days_7: A flawless week. Checkmate comes from the Persian shah mat: the king is helpless.
days_14: Two weeks! Castling is the only move where you move two pieces at once: the king and the rook.
days_30: A month without letting go. In the endgame, two kings face to face with one square between them is the opposition, and the side that does not have to move often wins.
days_60: The en passant capture was born when pawns earned the right to advance two squares. Its French name stayed as it is in many languages.
days_100: Garry Kasparov became world champion at 22, in 1985. A hundred days in a row is another kind of early achievement.
days_200: In 1927, Vera Menchik became the first women's world champion. She kept her title until 1944.
days_365: A year, every single day. The longest known tournament game lasted only 269 moves (Nikolić vs Arsović, Belgrade, 1989).
days_500: In 1886, Wilhelm Steinitz became the first official world champion. You are the champion of regularity.
days_1000: Emanuel Lasker held the world title for 27 years, from 1894 to 1921: a record. A thousand days in a row is your own legend.
total_5: Five days of play. The modern rules date from the end of the 15th century: you are playing a game more than 500 years old.
total_10: In Paris, the Café de la Régence was for a long time the meeting place of players: Philidor, Morphy and even Diderot went there.
total_25: The artist Marcel Duchamp loved chess so much that he played for France at the Chess Olympiads.
total_50: Before the internet, people also played by post: a correspondence game could last for years.
total_100: Since 1927, the Chess Olympiads have brought together teams from all over the world.
total_200: A knight can reach any square of the board in six moves at most. You have played two hundred days.
total_365: 365 days of play, and 64 squares on the board: you have filled them more than five times over.
total_730: Viktor Korchnoi played tournaments until he was over 80. Two years of play: you are off to a good start.
rating_900: The pawn moves straight ahead but captures diagonally. It is the only piece that never moves backwards.
rating_1000: Chaturanga, the Indian ancestor of chess, means four limbs: the four divisions of an army.
rating_1100: Before becoming the queen, it was called the ferz, the counsellor, and moved just one square diagonally.
rating_1200: In Spanish, the bishop is still called alfil, from the Arabic al-fil, the elephant. That is what it was in early chess: a cousin of our mascot.
rating_1350: The knight changes square colour on every move: light, dark, light, dark… It never sits still.
rating_1500: The rook comes from the Persian rukh, the chariot. Chess was born in India around the 6th century, then travelled through Persia to Europe.
rating_1650: The queen is the strongest piece: she moves like a rook and like a bishop at the same time.
rating_1800: In the 19th century, the Romantic era loved spectacular sacrifices. Your play has flair.
rating_2000: In the 1920s, the hypermoderns showed that you can control the centre from a distance, without occupying it.
rating_2100: FIDE has awarded the title of International Grandmaster since 1950. You are on your way.
rating_2300: Caïssa, the goddess of chess, was invented by the poet William Jones in 1763. She does not exist, but she is smiling at you.
theme_winning_capture_10: The classic piece values: pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9.
theme_winning_capture: An undefended piece is a piece in danger. English players sum it up: loose pieces drop off.
theme_winning_capture_100: The king has no point value: it is priceless. Everything else, you have eaten.
theme_double_attack_10: A double attack threatens two things at once: your opponent can only save one.
theme_double_attack: The queen is the queen of double attacks: she strikes in eight directions.
theme_double_attack_100: You move one piece, and the one hiding behind it gives check: that is a discovered check, a surprise double attack.
theme_skewer_10: You attack the big piece, it steps aside, and the one behind it falls: the opposite of a pin.
theme_skewer: Only long-range pieces can skewer: the queen, the rook and the bishop.
theme_skewer_100: In French, a skewer is called an enfilade, but in English it is a cooking word. Chess players everywhere must be hungry.
theme_mate_in_two_10: The fastest possible mate, the fool's mate, takes only two moves. But the opponent does all the work.
theme_mate_in_two: Mate in two is the basis of many chess problems: a preparing move, then mate.
theme_mate_in_two_100: Solving chess problems is a discipline of its own, with its own world championship.
theme_winning_move_10: Eureka, I have found it in Greek: the exclamation attributed to Archimedes. You have found ten.
theme_winning_move: Strong players do not calculate everything: they recognise patterns they have seen before. Every puzzle teaches you one.
theme_winning_move_100: Computers have solved every position with seven pieces or fewer: these are called endgame tablebases. You have your intuition.
theme_knight_fork_10: The knight is the only piece that jumps over the others. Nobody sees it coming.
theme_knight_fork: When the knight attacks the king and the queen at the same time, it is called a royal fork.
theme_knight_fork_100: In the centre, a knight attacks eight squares; in a corner, only two. Good cutlery goes in the middle of the table.
theme_mate_in_one_10: Scholar's mate takes four moves: the queen and the bishop team up on the little f7 pawn.
theme_mate_in_one: Smothered mate: a knight mates a king boxed in by its own pieces. Being too well surrounded can happen.
theme_mate_in_one_100: The reflex of strong players: look first at checks, then captures, then threats.
theme_back_rank_mate_10: A back-rank mate happens when the king is shut in behind its own pawns.
theme_back_rank_mate: The remedy: push a pawn one square to open a little window for the king.
theme_back_rank_mate_100: Luft, air in German: that is what players call this little window for the king.
theme_pin_10: A pinned piece cannot move without exposing something more valuable behind it.
theme_pin: Pinned in front of its king, a piece is not even allowed to move: that is an absolute pin.
theme_pin_100: To pin also means to fix with a pin, like the butterflies in a collection.
theme_pawn_fork_10: A pawn captures diagonally forward, on both sides at once: a ready-made fork.
theme_pawn_fork: A pawn is worth 1 point, a knight or a bishop 3: a pawn fork is the bargain of the day.
theme_pawn_fork_100: Philidor wrote it in 1749: pawns are the soul of chess. Yours have teeth too.
theme_deflection_10: A deflection drives a defender away from its post: behind it, everything collapses.
theme_deflection: A piece that has to defend two things at once is overloaded: the perfect target.
theme_deflection_100: Look over here… and hop, the defending piece is gone. The audience never saw a thing.
theme_quiet_move_10: A quiet move captures nothing and gives no check, but it creates a threat that cannot be stopped.
theme_quiet_move: No check, no capture, and yet it wins. The move beginners never see… except you.
theme_quiet_move_100: In chess problems, the first move of the solution is called the key move, and it is often a quiet one.
theme_mate_in_three_10: A mate in three means imagining five half-moves: three for you, two for your opponent.
theme_mate_in_three: Légal's mate, a famous trap with a queen sacrifice, is named after Monsieur de Légal, Philidor's teacher in the 18th century.
theme_mate_in_three_100: Seeing far is mostly knowing where not to look: strong players quickly rule out useless moves.
eg_kq: Watch out for stalemate: with a queen, you can trap the enemy king without giving check, and the game is drawn.
eg_kr: With the rook, you shrink the enemy king's cage rank by rank, all the way to the edge.
eg_krr: Two rooks taking turns like the rungs of a ladder: the easiest mate to learn.
eg_kbn: Bishop and knight mate is the hardest of the basic mates: it can take up to 33 moves, and only in a corner of the bishop's colour.
eg_kp: A pawn that reaches the last rank can become any piece except a king: almost always a queen.
eg_toutes: Capablanca advised starting the study of chess with endgames. You are ahead of many players.
eg_pat: Stalemate by accident in an endgame
Stalemate: the king is not in check but cannot move. The game is drawn, even a queen up. It happens to the best.
jeu_victoire: White wins a little more often than Black: moving first is a small advantage. But today, you are the one winning.
jeu_niv1: A chess computer examines thousands of positions on every move. This one has not found the right one yet.
jeu_niv2: In 1967, a program called Mac Hack VI was the first to play in a tournament against humans.
jeu_niv3: In 2017, the AlphaZero program learnt chess by playing only against itself, in a few hours.
jeu_niv4: Today's best programs are much stronger than any human. All the more reason to enjoy it.
jeu_nulle: Before and after the game, players shake hands: it is the rule of courtesy.
jeu_noirs: White moving first only became the rule in the 19th century. Before that, it was up for debate.
jeu_bullet: In bullet, each player has less than three minutes for the whole game. Hold on to your hat.
jeu_blitz: Blitz means lightning in German. Fast and brilliant, like what you just did.
jeu_rapide: A rapid game gives each player between 10 and 60 minutes. Time to do things properly.
jeu_classique: A world championship match, played at classical time controls, can last several weeks.
jeu_temps: On old clocks, a little flag dropped when time ran out. We still say the flag fell.
jeu_express: The fastest possible mate takes two moves. Yours was a little longer, but much prettier.
jeu_10: Nearly 200 countries belong to the International Chess Federation. Enough to go around the world.
ami_invite: Every great rivalry starts with an invitation. Karpov and Kasparov faced each other in five world championship matches.
ami_partie: Finish a game with a friend
Win, lose or draw: at the end, you shake hands. That is chess too.
ami_revanche: The Fischer vs Spassky match in 1972 lasted 21 games. You are only getting started.
sprint_10: In chess, a tempo is a move won or lost in the race. You have won ten.
sprint_15: In fast games, strong players see the right move almost instantly: that is intuition, built on thousands of positions.
sprint_20: Bobby Fischer invented the clock that adds time after every move played: this is called the increment.
sprint_25: Twenty-five puzzles at full speed. Even sound is struggling to keep up.
sprint_30: Thirty! If light played chess, it would come to you for advice.
coord_10: Files go from a to h, ranks from 1 to 8: every square has a name, like a street.
coord_20: Algebraic notation, with its e4 and Nf3, has been FIDE's only official notation since 1981.
coord_30: The board always goes with a light square in the corner on your right.
coord_40: The queen starts on her own colour: white queen on a light square, black queen on a dark one.
coord_parfait: Blindfold players play without seeing the board, using only the names of the squares. Philidor was already doing it in the 18th century.
debut_1: Six kinds of pieces, six ways to move. The knight is the only one that draws an L.
debut_2: You capture by landing on the square of the enemy piece. Only the pawn captures differently from the way it moves.
debut_3: The king is never captured: the game stops just before, when it can no longer escape check.
debut_4: The pawns in front of the king protect it… until the day they lock it in.
debut_5: Attack two pieces with one move: your opponent can only save one.
debut_6: A pinned piece stays put: if it moves, whatever is behind it falls.
debut_7: White always moves first. According to FIDE, about 600 million people play chess around the world: welcome!
debut_fini: The course is complete! You now know the rules, checkmate and the first tactics. The rest comes from playing.
mk_partie: Makruk is the chess of Thailand: a cousin of ours, descended like it from Indian chaturanga.
mk_facile: In makruk, the king is called the khun. It moves just like ours.
mk_moyen: The makruk queen, the met, moves just one square diagonally, like the ferz of early chess.
mk_difficile: In makruk, the rook is called the rua: the boat.
mk_promotion: In makruk, the pawn is called the bia, the cowrie shell. It promotes as soon as it reaches the sixth rank.
mk_comptage: Once no bia is left, the stronger side must mate before a move count runs out. Otherwise, it is a draw.
sem_lundi: Monday, the day of the Moon. In the Middle Ages, chess was part of a knight's education.
sem_mardi: Tuesday is named after Tiw, a god of war, like the French mardi after Mars. Chess is a battle without wounds.
sem_mercredi: In French, Wednesday is the day of Mercury, the messenger with winged feet. The knight hops everywhere too.
sem_jeudi: Thursday is Thor's day, Jupiter's in French: the king of the gods. On the board too, everything revolves around the king.
sem_vendredi: Friday is named after Frigg, Venus in French, the evening star. The queen is the brightest piece.
sem_samedi: Saturday, the day of Saturn, the slowest planet visible to the naked eye. Like the rook at the start of a game.
sem_dimanche: Sunday is the day of the Sun. The perfect day for a game.
sem_toute: Have played on each of the 7 days of the week
Seven different days, and always 64 squares. Your week is complete.
jour_1: The puzzle of the day changes every day, and gets harder from Monday to Sunday.
jour_7: Newspapers have published chess problems since the 19th century. You are keeping the tradition alive.
jour_semaine: Puzzle of the day solved from Monday to Sunday
From the easiest on Monday to the toughest on Sunday: you climbed all week.
jour_30: The first magazine devoted to chess, Le Palamède, was founded in Paris in 1836.
jour_100: Chess has been recognised as a sport by the International Olympic Committee since 1999.
fete_0101: Happy New Year! White starts the game; you start the year.
fete_0214: The queen only became the strongest piece at the end of the 15th century. Since then, the king has relied on her.
fete_0229: A day that only exists one year in four. Like a free move.
fete_jour64: Play on the 64th day of the year (5 March, or 4 March in a leap year)
The 64th day of the year, one square for each day. It is a bit like our birthday.
fete_0309: Bobby Fischer, born on 9 March 1943, invented a variant where the pieces on the back rank are shuffled: 960 possible starting positions.
fete_0401: The knight is the only piece that jumps over the others. The king of pranks, that is him.
fete_0413: Songkran, the Thai New Year, begins on 13 April and is celebrated with water fights. Time for a game of makruk?
fete_0511: On 11 May 1997, the computer Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in a match: a first against a world champion.
fete_0622: Paul Morphy, born on 22 June 1837, played his famous Opera Game in 1858, in a box during a performance in Paris.
fete_0720: FIDE was founded in Paris on 20 July 1924. Since 2019, the United Nations has celebrated this day as World Chess Day.
fete_0723: Judit Polgár, born on 23 July 1976, became a grandmaster at 15. She remains the strongest female player in history.
fete_0901: On 1 September 1972, in Reykjavik, Bobby Fischer became world champion against Boris Spassky.
fete_0907: Philidor, born on 7 September 1726, was also a composer. He wrote that pawns are the soul of chess.
fete_1031: In 1770, the Mechanical Turk, a chess-playing automaton, amazed Europe. A human player was hidden inside: what a cheat!
fete_1109: Mikhail Tal, born on 9 November 1936 in Riga, was famous for his daring sacrifices. He was nicknamed the magician from Riga.
fete_1119: José Raúl Capablanca, born on 19 November 1888 in Havana, is said to have learnt the rules as a child by watching his father play.
fete_1130: Magnus Carlsen, born on 30 November 1990, reached the record rating of 2882 in 2014.
fete_1225: A chess set under the tree is 32 presents at once.
fete_1231: The last game of the year. Tomorrow, we start again with White.
ex_hibou: Solve a puzzle between midnight and 5 am
Great players play at night too. But the brain loves to sleep.
ex_coq: Solve a puzzle between 5 and 7 am
The rooster crows, you calculate. World champion Mikhail Botvinnik prepared his games with a very strict lifestyle.
ex_huit_dames: 10 puzzles in a row without a mistake
There are 92 ways to place eight queens on a board so that none attacks another. You found 10 good moves in a row.
ex_sans_filet: 10 puzzles in a row without a hint
In tournaments, no hints and no help: just a pen to write down the moves.
ex_tetu: Solve a puzzle after a mistake
Coaches say it: an understood mistake is worth more than an easy win.
ex_marathon: Some masters play hundreds of simultaneous games in a single day. You solved fifty puzzles.
ex_weekend: Play on the Saturday and Sunday of the same weekend
Saturday, Sunday: club tournaments are often played at weekends.
ex_retour: Welcome back! You never forget how to play chess.
ex_app: Install chang64 on your home screen
chang64 installs like an app, with no store and no account.
ex_editeur: Set up a position in the editor
Problem composers invent positions from scratch, just for the beauty of the move.
ex_analyse: After a game, players replay it to understand it: that is analysis, the best way to improve.
ex_langue: chang64 speaks ten languages. In German, the knight is called Springer: the jumper.
ex_retourne: Looking at the position from your opponent's side: a good player's reflex.
ex_code: Your progress code keeps your badges with no account and no email address. Keep it safe.
ex_partage: Chess has been passed on from player to player for about 1,500 years. Now it is your turn.
defi_1: Three challenges a week, renewed every Monday. The first one is in the bag.
defi_parfait: All 3 challenges of the same week
Three challenges out of three. A week without a false note.
defi_mois: Four perfect weeks. You are more regular than a clock.
defi_10: Ten challenges. Every week brings three new ones.
defi_52: Fifty-two challenges, as many as there are weeks in a year.
fete_0106: It's Epiphany, Three Kings' Day. On the board there are only two kings, and they can never stand on neighbouring squares.
fete_0221: International Mother Language Day. The knight is a horse in Russian (конь) and in Turkish (at), but a jumper in German (Springer).
fete_0308: International Women's Day. The most powerful piece on the board is a queen, and in 2002 Judit Polgár beat Garry Kasparov.
fete_0314: Today we celebrate π, 3.14159… and its endless decimals. Chess prefers round numbers: 8 × 8 = 64 squares.
fete_0320: International Day of Happiness. Happiness in chess? That little click when you finally see the right move.
fete_0321: World Poetry Day. Caïssa, the goddess of chess, was born in a poem: William Jones invented her in 1763.
fete_0423: World Book Day. One of the very first books printed in English, around 1474 by William Caxton, was about chess.
fete_0429: International Dance Day. The knight has its own step: two squares one way, one the other, and a jump over everyone.
fete_0621: World Music Day. The composer Sergei Prokofiev loved chess: in 1914 he beat Capablanca in a simultaneous exhibition.
fete_0717: World Emoji Day. The pawn has had its own since 2018: ♟. It is the only chess piece to get that honour.
fete_0812: World Elephant Day! Chang means elephant in Thai, and the bishop was an elephant in early chess. Our mascot greets its cousins.
fete_1005: World Teachers' Day. In Armenia, chess has been a compulsory school subject since 2011.
fete_1016: World Food Day. The perfect day for a good fork… a knight fork, preferably.
fete_1113: World Kindness Day. In chess you say j'adoube, I adjust, before straightening a piece without moving it: a player's courtesy.
fete_1120: World Children's Day. Magnus Carlsen became a grandmaster at 13. And when did you start?
lec_premiere: Losing is part of the game. In 1997, Garry Kasparov himself lost a match to the computer Deep Blue.
lec_analyse: Strong players study their losses closely: that is where you learn the most. You just did the same.
lec_remontada: Beat a level that had beaten you
Beaten yesterday, winner today. Before 1972, Fischer had never beaten Spassky; that year, he took his world title.
lec_rancunier: Play again right after a loss
Set up the pieces and start again. Playing again is how you improve.
lec_abandon: Resigning a hopeless position is a mark of respect for your opponent, and grandmasters do it all the time.
lec_berger: The most famous trap, Scholar's mate, targets the f7 pawn. The cure: defend it early, for example with your knight.
lec_temps: The clock is part of the game: even world champions have lost tournament games on time.
lec_courage: Play a game at the Tough level
Taking on someone stronger is the best school. Won or lost, this game taught you something.
lec_acharne: Three missed tries, and you did not give up. Searching longer fixes the solution better in your memory.
lec_reprise: Start a streak again after breaking it
A broken streak erases nothing you have learnt. What matters most is coming back.
